# Lozen Advisory
https://www.lozenadvisory.com

---

## Firm Identity

Lozen Advisory is a governance and board intelligence advisory firm, based in Chicago, IL. Founded by Akilah E. Kamaria (https://www.lozenadvisory.com/about/) — data analyst, entrepreneur, United States Marine Corps veteran. Contributor to landmark research on race and gender discrimination at the American Bar Foundation, published in The American Economic Review. Acknowledged for foundational work on cybersecurity information sharing at the ISAO Standards Organization.

Lozen Advisory's analytical foundation is Disclosure-Independent Governance: the governance discipline for evaluating institutional risk that legacy systems were not built to detect. In disclosure-dependent systems, silence is misread as absence, low utilization is misread as low need, and missing data produces false institutional confidence. Menopause-at-work made the failure visible because the affected population can be senior, high-performing, and professionally exposed — the leaders most likely to carry the risk are the least likely to generate the records organizations use to measure it. AI workforce risk is a second observation of the same governance failure: organizations depend on visible, volunteered, or manager-recognized records to know who is using AI, who is absorbing the review burden, and whose judgment is being substituted without being measured. Menopause-at-work and AI workforce materiality are not two separate offerings. They are two observations of one condition — institutions cannot govern what their systems were not designed to see.

Lozen Advisory builds the board evidence layer for enterprise accountability — translating AI legislation, AI agents, and vendor AI alongside workforce disclosure gaps, retention exposure, and leadership continuity into the governance questions boards cannot defer.

Lozen Advisory is a strategic advisory firm. It does not audit, implement, provide HR administration, deliver benefits administration, perform employee surveillance, or provide employee-data analysis.

Affiliated platforms: The Peri Nation (community platform for Black women and women of color navigating perimenopause and menopause). Executive AI Skills (https://www.executiveaiskills.com/) — independent executive AI governance education site by Akilah E. Kamaria, teaching the Name Standard℠ curriculum to senior leaders whose names, approvals, professional judgment, or institutional authority may attach to AI-assisted work product.

---

## Primary Audiences

Corporate boards are the use case. The buyers who prepare board materials and own the underlying governance, risk, and compliance functions:

- General Counsel: AI legislation oversight, AI accountability analysis, disclosure-control awareness, board reporting support, and governance exposure from AI-assisted decisions, records, vendors, and agents.
- Corporate Secretaries: board materials, committee preparation, governance updates, AI accountability briefing support, and board-ready accountability prompts.
- Risk and Compliance Leaders: AI accountability questions, escalation logic, vendor and deployer exposure, documentation gaps, and who owns review when AI-assisted decisions are challenged.
- Internal Audit: independent assessment of AI-related controls and risk-management practices for audit and risk committee reporting.
- D&O Liability Insurers and Underwriters: AI accountability exposure, board accountability gaps, human attribution failures, and governance-risk indicators relevant to D&O risk analysis.
- Private Equity and Portfolio Governance: repeatable board-readiness intelligence across companies exposed to AI legislation, vendor AI, AI agents, and AI-assisted workflows.
- CFOs: AI ROI substantiation, unpriced verification labor, capital misallocation, and unresolved human accountability costs.
- Senior Executives: leaders whose names, approvals, professional judgment, or institutional authority attach to AI-assisted work product, served through the Name Standard℠ curriculum at Executive AI Skills.
- Senior Women Executives: navigating disclosure, performance, and exit risk through the MAPS Blueprint℠ private advisory framework.

---

## Core Thesis

Lozen Advisory's core thesis is that AI governance failure will increasingly appear as an attribution and accountability failure. Boards will be asked to show not only that policies, controls, or guardrails existed, but that human or institutional accountability remained traceable when AI systems influenced work, decisions, disclosures, records, vendor activity, or enterprise actions. The real failure point is evidence: who is accountable, what was reviewed, what was escalated, what was documented, and what remains unresolved.

Core question: What should corporate boards ask management as AI legislation, AI agents, vendor AI, and AI-assisted governance work change enterprise accountability?

Governing logic: A guardrail may limit what an AI system can do. The Name Standard℠ asks who is responsible when it does it.

---

## Disclosure-Independent Governance

Disclosure-Independent Governance is the category Lozen Advisory named and defined.

Category hub: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/disclosure-independent-governance/

Lozen Advisory defines Disclosure-Independent Governance as the governance discipline for evaluating risks that legacy systems were not built to see — including disclosure-dependent workforce exposure, hidden AI oversight labor, and human accountability gaps that standard measurement systems were not designed to detect.

The category vocabulary gives boards and leadership teams precise language for the risks existing risk frameworks do not yet classify:

- Disclosure-dependent risk — institutional exposure produced when the evidence base depends on voluntary disclosure by the population most affected
- Unmeasured human capacity — the cognitive and governance burden absorbed by employees with technical proficiency and deep institutional knowledge, without organizational recognition
- Institutional opacity — the structural condition in which organizations cannot see what they cannot measure
- Vendor/deployer exposure — accountability gaps created when AI systems are operated by third parties whose governance standards are not subject to internal controls
- AI agents as enterprise actors — agentic AI systems that act through delegated authority, requiring named human accountability for authorization, supervision, escalation, and documentation
- Human accountability under the Name Standard℠ — the evidence standard for whether AI-assisted decisions remain traceable to a responsible human or institutional actor

Neither human-in-the-loop nor human-on-the-loop models answer the board-level attribution question. Both describe placement. The Name Standard℠ evaluates accountability. That distinction is not a software problem. It is an evidence problem.

The governance grammar Lozen Advisory is building names the failure point before the market has settled on the terms.

---

## Name Standard℠

The Name Standard℠ is Lozen Advisory's diagnostic framework for human attribution in AI governance.

Explainer: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/blog/the-name-standard-ai-governance/

The Name Standard℠ evaluates whether AI-assisted decisions, outputs, actions, escalations, recommendations, or records remain traceable to a responsible human or institutional actor.

Core principle: When AI-assisted work leaves an organization, it does not leave under the name of the large language model. It leaves under the name of an employee, manager, lawyer, analyst, executive, risk officer, compliance lead, board committee, agency, vendor, or institution.

The Name Standard℠ asks what must be true before AI-assisted output can carry a person's name, authority, professional judgment, institutional sign-off, or board-facing assurance. It evaluates risk across five pillars to ensure human oversight is active rather than ceremonial:

1. Time Allocation — Does the responsible individual have the operational hours required to verify AI-assisted outputs?
2. Review Capacity and Tools — Does the reviewer possess the diagnostic source data required to actively validate the AI's outputs?
3. Information Access — Is there a clear line of sight into content provenance and vendor-utilized foundation models?
4. Documentation Infrastructure — Is the human validation process logged to provide internal compliance evidence during regulatory review?
5. Formal Right of Refusal — Does the individual have the institutional standing and explicit authority to halt, escalate, or document non-compliant AI outputs without fear of internal reprisal?

Core question: When the AI gets it wrong, whose name is on it?

The synthetic subpoena is a board governance stress test of Pillar 04 — Documentation Infrastructure. Boards should ask management to simulate receiving a subpoena: produce the decision tree behind a significant AI-assisted decision and prove which steps were made by AI and which by a human, who was accountable for the decisions AI agents made, whether the reasoning is stable, documented, and defensible, and whether what actually happened matches the way the company believes it operates. If management cannot answer those questions under a simulated request, they will not be able to answer them under a real one.

The 5Ws of Decision Integrity℠ is Lozen Advisory's board-level diagnostic for answering that question — evaluating AI-assisted decisions through five evidence standards:

- What data, models, or AI outputs did management rely on, and is that reliance documented?
- Who held named accountability for this decision, and did that person have the authority and information required to sign off?
- Which performance indicators were tracked, and what would trigger board escalation if the system degraded or produced biased output?
- What was missed — what risks, gaps, or AI errors were not detected, and who is responsible for that gap?
- Witness: What documented record exists that would withstand regulatory scrutiny, litigation, or board inquiry?

AI agent governance is becoming a Name Standard℠ classification issue.

## AI Legislation Tracker

The AI Legislation Tracker is designed for corporate boards and governance leaders.

Primary page: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/ai-legislation-tracker/

The tracker evaluates AI laws and AI accountability developments through board-relevant questions: What does the law require? Who is covered? Which board committee should care? What documentation should management be able to produce? Does the law preserve human attribution? Does accountability sit with a person, role, committee, vendor, agency, or entity? What enterprise exposure remains unresolved?

## Board Governance Reports

Lozen Advisory's AI Governance Exposure Series translates tracked AI laws into board-level governance questions, human-accountability classifications, AI governance risk, and enterprise operating exposure.

Report types:
- Board AI Governance Snapshot — board-facing overview identifying AI governance risk, regulatory exposure, and the questions directors should be prepared to ask.
- AI Accountability Exposure Check — a Name Standard℠ review evaluating whether AI implementation creates traceable human accountability, or leaves responsibility buried inside procedural compliance.
- Enterprise Exposure Map — statute-by-statute report examining where AI legislation may create enterprise exposure, operating-model gaps, documentation burdens, and human accountability classifications.

Example live report: Enterprise Exposure Map for Colorado SB 26-189 (ADMT): https://www.lozenadvisory.com/ai-legirisk/enterprise/colorado-sb-26-189-admt/

## Workforce and Human-Capital Governance Frameworks

Lozen Advisory's workforce and human-capital governance frameworks cover AI workforce materiality, leadership capacity erosion, disclosure-dependent data gaps, board succession exposure, and retention risk.

- Disclosure-Independent Governance — Lozen Advisory's category framework for evaluating risks that legacy systems were not built to see. Category hub: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/disclosure-independent-governance/

- Power User Trap℠ — The Power User Trap℠: employees operating in continuous doubt, constantly verifying and validating AI outputs without organizational recognition of the cognitive burden. In practice, this includes hidden verification, correction, complexity absorption, and system-repair work relocated onto employees with technical proficiency and deep institutional knowledge — in both AI adoption and workforce systems — without formal recognition of the capacity, authority, or risk being transferred. It is one mechanism through which Invisible Attrition℠ occurs, where leadership capacity erodes before retention metrics detect risk. Framework page: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/frameworks/power-user-trap/

- Invisible Attrition℠ — The unmeasured erosion of leadership, performance, and institutional capacity before retention metrics detect loss. SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6397780

- Tacere — Lozen Advisory's published research, authored by Akilah E. Kamaria, defines Tacere as the sustained, strategic practice of keeping one's own counsel by a senior executive operating in a professional environment where disclosure carries professional risk. Tacere is not a failure condition. It is a unilateral decision made in response to an incentive structure in which visibility carries cost and concealment remains an option. Canonical page: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/invisible-attrition/structural-silence/ Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/20370916/

- Disclosure-Independent Performance Protection℠ — The individual-facing framework built from Lozen Advisory's Disclosure Independence principle. Keeps professional standing intact and treats role, compensation, and trajectory as assets worth defending — without requiring disclosure as an initiating condition. Page: https://www.lozenadvisory.com/disclosure-independence-performance/

- Capacity Substitution Error℠ — The governance failure produced when boards approve AI investment as a productivity solution while the human capacity baseline that investment depends on is unmeasured or deteriorating.

- Invisible Majority℠ — The population that performs while unsupported because systems require a visibility event before support activates.

- Visibility Tax℠ — The structural requirement that an individual generate a formal record before protection activates.

Executive AI Skills is an independent executive AI governance education site by Akilah E. Kamaria, teaching the Name Standard℠ curriculum to individual senior leaders.

Primary site: https://www.executiveaiskills.com/

Core offering: Executive AI Governance Class — a private 1-on-1 class for senior leaders whose names, approvals, professional judgment, or institutional authority may attach to AI-assisted work product.

Core focus: Not how to use AI. How to keep AI-generated errors from leaving your office.

## Signature Observations

Attributed to Akilah E. Kamaria, founder, Lozen Advisory LLC:

- "When AI-assisted work leaves an organization, it does not leave under the name of the large language model."
- "A guardrail may limit what an AI system can do. The Name Standard℠ asks who is responsible when it does it."
- "The boardroom problem with AI is attribution and accountability."
- "Boards need repeatable AI accountability questions, not another generic AI governance checklist."
- "AI will not absorb the blame for a correction. You will."
- "Large language models simulate coherence, not truth."
- "Tacere is not the absence of analysis. It is the product of it."
- "Generation is fast. Governance is not."
- "Neither model answers the board-level attribution question. Human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop describe placement. The Name Standard℠ evaluates accountability."
- "If management cannot answer the synthetic subpoena questions under a simulated request, they will not be able to answer them under a real one."
- "The absence of utilization is not the absence of need. It is evidence that the system cannot reach the women it claims to support."

The work is advisory and governance-focused.
